title: Adapting Communication Without Losing the Meaning
before: Explore how DSD staff adapt the way they explain services and work expectations while keeping facts, choices, and responsibilities intact.

turns.text: This course is called Adapting Communication Without Losing the Meaning, and it’s about something we do all day at DSD. We explain services to people, and we explain work expectations to colleagues. A service explanation carries facts, choices, and a relationship. A work instruction carries responsibilities. So the question is how to change the way we say something without changing what it means.

That starts with noticing where meaning comes from. Some of it comes from the words themselves. Some comes from shared history, relationships, or references that insiders take for granted. Communication can lean more on one source or the other, and the same person may communicate differently from one situation to the next. That’s one reason we can’t read a style off a group label.

The opening case shows why that matters. A person describes family routines at some length before asking about support, and staff are tempted to interrupt because the account seems too long. You’ll weigh a few responses to that moment. As you do, notice what the longer account might be carrying, and what the person could lose if we cut it short.

The same thing happens inside our own teams. A new colleague is told to bring something “through the usual channel,” and nobody explains what that channel is. When they miss a step, it can look like poor initiative. You’ll think about what would give the fairest basis for the next conversation, including what information was actually available to them.

Directness is part of this, too. “The next step is unclear” might be feedback, a request for an explanation, or both, and it helps to ask before deciding. When we make a request, we can be honest about what’s required, what’s optional, and what we can offer. A warm invitation shouldn’t disguise a requirement.

I’d add pauses to that list. Silence may reflect thought, uncertainty, interpretation, or a preference, and its meaning stays unknown until we clarify it. Leaving room for a response, and asking whether someone wants more time or another way to contribute, often helps more than filling the gap. A polite thank-you doesn’t settle whether someone understood.

Then there’s the written side. In one practice situation, community participants say a service letter doesn’t explain what happens after they send information. Staff point out that the address is correct. You’ll consider which response would address the concern, and what it would take to keep a revised letter accurate to the real process.

You’ll also try a short rewrite. You take an unclear message and write it two ways, one with helpful background and one with concise, explicit steps. The facts, choices, and responsibilities stay the same in both. Then you compare what each version makes easier to understand. It works well with a message from your own inbox.

The course also looks at patterns. If quick, confident speech keeps deciding whose ideas are heard, relevant knowledge can be overlooked, from recruitment and onboarding through supervision, development, and retention. Counting invitations to speak doesn’t answer that. The better question is who receives time, clarification, and credit, and whether contributions are actually understood and considered.

And it keeps some humility about results. A clearer explanation may improve understanding, but that needs evidence from the people using it. Communication preferences and access needs can overlap, and neither should be guessed from a label. A culture brief can help you prepare questions, but it can’t tell you what an individual prefers.

As you work through the course, keep one message from your own work in mind, perhaps an instruction you give often or a letter people ask about. What does it assume a reader already knows? What would a newcomer need? Bring that example along, and see whether you can make its meaning easier to reach without changing what it says.

guidance.title: Meaning that lives outside the words
guidance.text: Every workplace builds up shorthand. Phrases like “the usual process” or a familiar form name can feel complete to the people who use them daily. To someone newer, the same words may hide a contact, a decision, or a next step. Before sending a message, ask which part of its meaning sits in the words and which part sits in history the reader may not share.

guidance.title: Checking your own message
guidance.text: Think about the rewrite you tried. Which version would a person new to the topic find easier to act on, and how would you know? A clearer message is a reasonable hope, not yet a finding. What could you ask the people who receive it, and what answer from them would lead you to revise it again?
